gis_source: Duke project maps / DEP siting records
source_excerpt: “For hurricanes Milton and Helene, I remained in a storm role for over two weeks before taking time off to repair my home. Working through storm restoration, especially while handling personal impacts, is never easy but we proudly work to restore communities as quickly as possible, because this is the place we call home too.” Staying ahead of future storms Physical infrastructure upgrades occur year-round to strengthen the poles and wires and reduce outages. Approximately 60% of wooden transmission poles have been upgraded to stronger materials over the last five years and approximately 50% of the distribution system is now underground. Vegetation trimming is also a critical piece of storm preparation. Each year, thousands of miles of trees are pruned along the power lines, helping to prevent vegetation-caused outages. Our view: “In the aftermath of a storm, our teams work incredibly hard around the clock to restore our customer’s power,” said Melissa Seixas, Duke Energy Florida state president.

Since transmission line corridors can be up to a mile wide and several hundred miles long, many alternates can be proposed and must be reviewed. source_excerpt: 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act, 15 U.S.C. Applicants (see NGTPSA application guide ) may use the licensing process under the NGTPSA for projects exempt from the Act (see NGTPSA applicability flow chart ). Certification Process for Transmission Pipelines: The certification process and procedural requirements ( see NGTPSA certification process flow chart ) are similar to those for electrical transmission lines, including the ability of parties to propose alternate corridors and the possibility that an alternate corridor will be the one certified. A difference between the two Acts is that electrical transmission corridors can be up to a mile wide, while under the NGTPSA, corridors can only be one-third mile wide. This reduces the amount of area to be reviewed and the number of people who may potentially be affected by the pipeline. As with transmission lines, safety and land ownership questions frequently arise about natural gas pipeline location.

project_name: Building a new substation
source_excerpt: Please refer to the project map. Tampa Electric is: Building a new substation on Cass Street, near Nebraska Avenue, on the north end of downtown. Installing a new underground power line running west for three blocks along Cass Street, and then south on Jefferson Street for about a quarter-mile, connecting to Tampa Electric's existing Washington Street Substation. Building a new overhead power line running east for two blocks along Cass Street and crossing the railroad tracks to Union Station. The new steel poles will be up to 120 feet tall and about 36 inches wide at ground level. Construction began in May 2024 and is expected to be completed by January 2027.

source_excerpt: Tampa Electric Forms DO NOT use this form to report downed or fallen streetlights, power lines or poles. Those are electric emergencies. To report a downed or damaged power line, call 911 and then call us at 877-588-1010 . Always assume downed power lines and poles are energized and stay as far away as possible! DO NOT TOUCH them - or anyone or anything touching them - such as a tree branch, fence, vehicle or water. Streetlight Outage Reporting Please complete this form to report a malfunctioning streetlight.
